name: Tibial Bone Stress Injury
summary: Load-related tibial bone stress continuum from periosteal reaction to stress fracture, often associated with abrupt increases in running or impact.

looksLike: Focal or diffuse tibial pain with running
Pain may progress from exercise-only to walking/rest
redFlags: Pain at rest/night or inability to bear weight
Anterior tibial cortex focal pain (higher-risk site)
Low energy availability or bone-health concerns
firstSteps: Stop running/jumping that provokes bone pain
Maintain pain-free cross-training only if medically appropriate
Assess footwear, training error, nutrition and bone-health risk

assess: Pain with impact may occur but hopping is not a safe exclusion test
Gait change in more advanced injury

tests.name: Clinical Tibial Palpation and Load History
tests.purpose: Map tenderness distribution and relate symptoms to recent impact exposure; no single field test rules out stress injury.
tests.positive: Focal bony tenderness with progressive impact-related pain or high-risk history.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Stop running/jumping that provokes bone pain
Maintain pain-free cross-training only if medically appropriate
Assess footwear, training error, nutrition and bone-health risk
Use protected weight bearing if walking is painful and clinician advises
dose: No impact exercise while walking or daily activity remains painful
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Begin progressive strength and low-impact conditioning when daily walking is pain-free
Reintroduce impact only after clinical criteria and risk-site review
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Graded walk-run programme with rest days
Monitor focal pain during and after loading
dose: Walk-run intervals on alternate days, starting short
Increase one variable at a time; regress if focal bone pain returns
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: No focal bony tenderness as judged clinically
Risk site and imaging/medical review addressed

structures: Tibial cortex and periosteum; anterior cortex and high-risk sites require particular caution.
mechanism: Low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction, low bone density or inadequate recovery may increase risk
classification: Bone stress reaction to stress fracture continuum
Low-risk posteromedial tibia versus higher-risk anterior cortex
investigations: MRI is preferred when early bone stress injury is suspected and diagnosis affects management; radiographs may initially be normal.
Assess bone-health and energy-availability risk factors with appropriate clinicians.
manual: Manual therapy does not heal bone stress injury and should not be applied over a suspected fracture.
Address only secondary mobility deficits after medical clearance.
modalities: No modality substitutes for load reduction, bone-health assessment and graded return.
Avoid using analgesia to mask pain and continue impact.
mistakes: Using hop test to rule out fracture
Continuing impact through focal bone pain
Ignoring energy availability and bone-health risk
pearls: Anterior tibial cortex is a higher-risk location than posteromedial tibia.
A normal early radiograph does not exclude bone stress injury.

tests.name: Clinical Tibial Palpation and Load History
tests.purpose: Map tenderness distribution and relate symptoms to recent impact exposure; no single field test rules out stress injury.
tests.positive: Focal bony tenderness with progressive impact-related pain or high-risk history.
tests.patientPosition: Review training history and palpate tibia systematically; avoid repeated hopping if stress fracture is suspected.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Stop impact loading and arrange medical assessment/imaging when bone stress injury is suspected.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
